title: Canonical tensor isomorphism for a right coideal subalgebra
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], $H$ a commutative Hopf $k$-algebra, and $A\subseteq H$ a unital right coideal subalgebra, meaning $\Delta(A)\subseteq A\otimes_kH$. Use the Hopf identities, quotient coalgebra $C=H/HA^+$, quotient map $\pi$, and notion of relative Hopf module of [lem-sfb-relative-hopf-module-kernels]. For every left $H$-module $X$, give $C\otimes_kX$ the diagonal action $h(c\otimes x)=\sum h_{(1)}c\otimes h_{(2)}x$ and coaction $\Delta_C\otimes1_X$. Regard $X$ as an $A$-module by restriction, so that $H\otimes_AX=L(X)$ is the relative Hopf module of [lem-sfb-relative-hopf-module-kernels]. The map $\kappa_X:H\otimes_AX\to C\otimes_kX$, $h\otimes x\mapsto\sum\pi(h_{(1)})\otimes h_{(2)}x$, is an isomorphism of relative Hopf modules. Its inverse is the well-defined map $\pi(h)\otimes x\mapsto\sum h_{(1)}\otimes S(h_{(2)})x$. The maps $\kappa_X$ are natural for $H$-linear maps of $X$.

source.place: Bichon, arXiv:2301.05480v2, Proposition 2.2, canonical isomorphism and its displayed inverse. Read at https://arxiv.org/html/2301.05480v2; local PDF WANTED in report.md.

proof.text: Use the quotient, actions and Hopf identities of [lem-sfb-relative-hopf-module-kernels] and the tensor universal property of [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. Throughout, Sweedler sums mean applying the displayed linear maps to finite tensor expansions, not choosing components canonically. For $a\in A$ and $t\in H$, $a-\epsilon(a)1\in A^+$ gives $\pi(ta)=\epsilon(a)\pi(t)$. Since $\pi$ is onto and $\Delta$ is multiplicative, the quotient formula gives $\Delta_C(hc)=\sum h_{(1)}c_{(1)}\otimes h_{(2)}c_{(2)}$ and $\epsilon_C(hc)=\epsilon(h)\epsilon_C(c)$, by writing $c=\pi(t)$. These identities require no antipode stability of $A$.

source.place: Bichon, arXiv:2301.05480v2, section 2.2, Proposition 2.2 and its displayed inverse; expanded tensor calculations by Q53. HTML read at https://arxiv.org/html/2301.05480v2; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: The proposed diagonal action on $C\otimes_kX$ is a unital associative action: applying $g$ after $h$ gives $\sum g_{(1)}h_{(1)}c\otimes g_{(2)}h_{(2)}x=(gh)(c\otimes x)$, since $\Delta$ is an algebra map; the unit acts identically. Set $\alpha=\Delta_C\otimes1_X$. Its coassociativity and counit equations are those of $C$, tensored with $X$. The identity in step 1 gives $\alpha(h(c\otimes x))=\sum h_{(1)}c_{(1)}\otimes h_{(2)}c_{(2)}\otimes h_{(3)}x=\sum h_{(1)}(c\otimes x)_{(-1)}\otimes h_{(2)}(c\otimes x)_{(0)}$. Thus this is precisely a relative Hopf module in the cited definition.

source.place: Bichon, arXiv:2301.05480v2, section 2.2, Proposition 2.2 and its displayed inverse; expanded tensor calculations by Q53. HTML read at https://arxiv.org/html/2301.05480v2; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Define the $k$-bilinear expression $F(h,x)=\sum\pi(h_{(1)})\otimes h_{(2)}x$. For $a\in A$, expand $\Delta(a)$ in $A\otimes_kH$. Step 1 and the counit identity give $F(ha,x)=\sum\pi(h_{(1)})\epsilon(a_{(1)})\otimes h_{(2)}a_{(2)}x=F(h,ax)$. Moreover $F(gh,x)=\sum\pi(g_{(1)}h_{(1)})\otimes g_{(2)}h_{(2)}x=gF(h,x)$. In particular for $g\in A$ this and balancing make $F$ bilinear over $A$ for the restricted diagonal action on the target. The tensor universal property therefore gives the stated $H$-linear map $\kappa_X:H\otimes_AX\to C\otimes_kX$.

source.place: Bichon, arXiv:2301.05480v2, section 2.2, Proposition 2.2 and its displayed inverse; expanded tensor calculations by Q53. HTML read at https://arxiv.org/html/2301.05480v2; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Define $G(h,x)=\sum h_{(1)}\otimes_A S(h_{(2)})x$, a $k$-bilinear expression. For $a\in A$, expand $\Delta(a)$ with first factors in $A$ and use that $S$ is an algebra map in the commutative Hopf convention of the cited node. Balancing over $A$ and commutativity of $H$ give $G(ha,x)=\sum h_{(1)}a_{(1)}\otimes_A S(h_{(2)})S(a_{(2)})x=\sum h_{(1)}\otimes_A a_{(1)}S(a_{(2)})S(h_{(2)})x=\epsilon(a)G(h,x)$. Hence $G(ha,x)=0$ for $a\in A^+$. Every element of $J=HA^+$ is a finite sum of such products, so $G(J,x)=0$. The expression factors through $H/J$ in its first variable and then, by the tensor universal property over $k$, defines $\lambda_X:C\otimes_kX\to H\otimes_AX$ with exactly the required formula. This descent uses neither $S(A)\subseteq A$ nor any flatness assumption.

source.place: Bichon, arXiv:2301.05480v2, section 2.2, Proposition 2.2 and its displayed inverse; expanded tensor calculations by Q53. HTML read at https://arxiv.org/html/2301.05480v2; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Coassociativity and the identity $\mu(S\otimes1)\Delta=\eta\epsilon$ from the cited Hopf axioms yield $\lambda_X\kappa_X(h\otimes_Ax)=\sum h_{(1)}\otimes_A S(h_{(2)})h_{(3)}x=\sum h_{(1)}\otimes_A\epsilon(h_{(2)})x=h\otimes_Ax$. Here the antipode identity contracts the last two factors of $(1\otimes\Delta)\Delta(h)$; the last equality is the counit identity. Pure tensors generate, so $\lambda_X\kappa_X=1$.

source.place: Bichon, arXiv:2301.05480v2, section 2.2, Proposition 2.2 and its displayed inverse; expanded tensor calculations by Q53. HTML read at https://arxiv.org/html/2301.05480v2; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: The other antipode identity $\mu(1\otimes S)\Delta=\eta\epsilon$ gives $\kappa_X\lambda_X(\pi(h)\otimes x)=\sum\pi(h_{(1)})\otimes h_{(2)}S(h_{(3)})x=\sum\pi(h_{(1)})\otimes\epsilon(h_{(2)})x=\pi(h)\otimes x$. Surjectivity of $\pi$ and generation by pure tensors imply $\kappa_X\lambda_X=1$. Thus the two displayed, well-defined maps are inverse $k$-linear maps.

source.place: Bichon, arXiv:2301.05480v2, section 2.2, Proposition 2.2 and its displayed inverse; expanded tensor calculations by Q53. HTML read at https://arxiv.org/html/2301.05480v2; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: The coaction on $L(X)$ supplied by the cited node and coassociativity give $(1_C\otimes\kappa_X)\alpha_{L(X)}(h\otimes_Ax)=\sum\pi(h_{(1)})\otimes\pi(h_{(2)})\otimes h_{(3)}x=\alpha\kappa_X(h\otimes_Ax)$. Thus $\kappa_X$ is a relative Hopf-module morphism. Its inverse is $H$-linear: apply injective $\kappa_X$ to $\lambda_X(hz)$ and $h\lambda_X(z)$, and both images are $hz$. Similarly, composing the coaction equation with $\lambda_X$ on the domain and then $1_C\otimes\lambda_X$ on the codomain gives $\alpha_{L(X)}\lambda_X=(1_C\otimes\lambda_X)\alpha$. Hence $\lambda_X$ is also a relative Hopf-module morphism.

source.place: Bichon, arXiv:2301.05480v2, section 2.2, Proposition 2.2 and its displayed inverse; expanded tensor calculations by Q53. HTML read at https://arxiv.org/html/2301.05480v2; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: For any $H$-linear $f:X\to Y$, it is $A$-linear on restriction, so the cited induction construction gives $L(f)=1_H\otimes_Af$. On generators, $(1_C\otimes f)\kappa_X(h\otimes_Ax)=\sum\pi(h_{(1)})\otimes f(h_{(2)}x)=\sum\pi(h_{(1)})\otimes h_{(2)}f(x)=\kappa_YL(f)(h\otimes_Ax)$. Also $1_C\otimes f$ commutes with the diagonal action by $H$-linearity of $f$ and with $\Delta_C\otimes1$ by its formula, so the naturality square lies in relative Hopf modules. This proves the stated natural isomorphism.

Step 3: kappa is balanced over A because a1 is in A, and it is H-linear. Step 4: the inverse lambda vanishes on HA+, because G(ha,x)=eps(a)G(h,x); this uses that S is an algebra map, that H is commutative, mu(1⊗S)Delta=eta eps, and moving a1 in A across ⊗_A; it does not need S(A)⊆A. Steps 5-6: both composites are the identity, by the two antipode identities and coassociativity. Step 7: kappa and lambda commute with the coactions. Step 8: naturality. The two cited statements (lem-sfb-relative-hopf-module-kernels, same unit; def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product, a Mathlib definition over a commutative ring, which covers ⊗_A) say what each step takes from them. Marking the steps elementary is justified. proof_deps equals the union of uses.
